extracted.intended_audience: readers of satirical literature; translators; literary critics; general educated public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative commentary on translating, prefacing, and presenting satirical works (exemplified by Rabelais), plus related remarks on who will appreciate such works and on physicians' comportment (anecdotal).

rubrics_metrics.name: What pleases a reasonable reader
rubrics_metrics.description: If uncommon worth, lively wit, and deep learning, wove into wholesome satire, a bold, good, and vast design admirably pursued, truth set out in its true light, and a method how to arrive to its oracle, can recommend a work, I am sure this has enough to please any reasonable man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The translator/author argues these combined qualities (worth, wit, learning, wholesome satire, clear presentation of truth, and method) constitute sufficient recommendation; contrasts this with other works "in the French" that are more obvious and entertaining but come far short in certain respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's proper claim to praise
rubrics_metrics.description: The first [translator] pretends to much praise, besides that of giving his author’s sense in its full extent, and copying his style, if it is to be copied; since he has no share in the invention or disposition of what he translates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator's legitimate aims are fidelity to author's sense and, where appropriate, reproduction of style; translator should not claim credit for invention or arrangement of material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a translation read like a free, easy original
rubrics_metrics.description: It cannot be easy to give it the free easy air of an original; for even what seems most common talk in one language, is what is often the most difficult to be made so in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator must wrestle with obsolete words, turns of phrase, and darkly treated subjects; aim for natural, idiomatic English rather than slavish word-for-word rendering. Examples and classical allusions (Horace) support this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overvalue matching cant or slang vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Far be it from me, for all this, to value myself upon hitting the words of cant in which my drolling author is so luxuriant; for though such words have stood me in good stead, I scarce can forbear thinking myself unhappy in having insensibly hoarded up so much gibberish and Billingsgate trash in my memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid thinking fluency in slang or cant is a mark of success; matching obscure or foul terms is not necessarily praiseworthy. Translator should exercise judgment rather than merely compile 'fripperies.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefatory apologies are useless if the work fails
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be needless to give here a large account of my performance; for, after all, you readers care no more for this or that apology, or pretence of Mr. Translator, if the version does not please you, than we do for a blundering cook’s excuse after he has spoiled a good dish in the dressing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/translators should not expect apologies or long defenses in a preface to substitute for producing a pleasing version; the work itself determines readers' acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirist may obscure or droll to avoid persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabelais to study to be dark, and even bedaub it with many loose expressions, that he might not be thought to have any other design than to droll; in a manner bewraying his book that his enemies might not bite it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate obscurity, loose or playful expressions can be a protective device for satire — masking direct attack to avoid enemies. This is presented as an explanation of Rabelais' style and a permissible tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended audience for this kind of mirth
rubrics_metrics.description: This work cannot miss being liked by those who are for witty mirth and a chirping bottle; though not by those solid sots who seem to have drudged all their youth long only that they might enjoy the sweet blessing of getting drunk every night in their old age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humorous, satirical works of this tone will please readers who relish lively wit and convivial mirth rather than solemn, dour, or overly sober audiences. Know your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuking critics who do not produce
rubrics_metrics.description: If thou art one of those who, though they never write, criticise everyone that does; avaunt!—Thou art a professed enemy of mankind and of thyself, who wilt never be pleased nor let anybody be so, and knowest no better way to fame than by striving to lessen that of others; though wouldst thou write thou mightst be soon known...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text denounces professional detractors and idle critics: critique without production is portrayed as malicious or vain. As an evaluative norm, prefer makers over mere fault-finders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician's demeanor toward patients
rubrics_metrics.description: Above all things, the forecited authors have given particular directions to physicians about the words, discourse, and converse which they ought to have with their patients; everyone aiming at one point, that is, to rejoice them without offending God, and in no wise whatsoever to vex or displease them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance drawn from Hippocrates and other authorities: physicians should cultivate pleasant countenance and discourse to comfort patients; being morose or insulting is an anti-pattern (examples of rude physician replies are cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of bad physician speech as anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Callianax, asked 'Shall I die?' answered 'Patroclus died, whom all allow By much a better man than you.' Another: asked 'Does my water tell you I shall die?' replied 'No; if Latona... begot thee.' Galen blames Quintus who, told 'your breath smells of wine,' retorted 'Yours smells of fever.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These anecdotes are presented as condemnations of arrogant, flippant, or cruel medical replies; they serve as cautionary exemplars of what physicians should not say to patients.
